questions.question: Why does every backend call the same render_tile function?
questions.short: Every backend only decides who renders which tile and when; they all call the same render_tile. So a backend that changed the image would have a bug, which makes exact image equality a correctness test.
evidence: Seven backends produce hash 57881d257daf2474 for the showcase configuration
validate_backends.py: 11 configurations, one hash
questions.caveat: Exact equality holds for this build; a different compiler could need a tolerance check.

questions.question: Why use deterministic per-sample random numbers?
questions.short: Each sample seeds its own generator from (seed, pixel, sample), so a pixel's random numbers do not depend on which thread or rank renders it. A shared generator would change the image whenever scheduling changed.
evidence: Rng{mix64(seed ^ mix64(pixel) ^ mix64(sample))} in render_tile
Samples are accumulated in a fixed order; each pixel has one writer
questions.caveat: Determinism removes Monte Carlo noise from comparisons; it does not make timing deterministic.

questions.question: Why use MPI when everything runs on one machine?
questions.short: MPI models distributed memory: separate processes, explicit messages and a coordinator. On one host it measures the programming model and scheduling protocol, not a network.
evidence: MPI 4 ranks: 1.95× (static partition)
Coordinator/worker protocol with MPI_ANY_SOURCE
questions.caveat: No network latency or bandwidth effect was measured; the results do not predict cluster behaviour.

questions.question: Why do 8 OpenMP threads improve runtime but reduce efficiency?
questions.short: Eight logical threads run on four physical cores. SMT lets a second thread use execution resources the first leaves idle, so runtime drops, but a hyperthread is not a second core, so efficiency per logical processor falls.
evidence: OpenMP 8 1.323 s vs OpenMP 4 2.041 s: -34.69% (7/7 blocks)
Efficiency: OpenMP 4 0.48, OpenMP 8 0.37 per logical processor
questions.caveat: Why this workload benefits (for example memory stalls in BVH traversal) was not measured.

questions.question: Why combine MPI and OpenMP?
questions.short: MPI distributes tiles between processes and OpenMP splits each tile between threads. Varying ranks × threads with the rendering code fixed shows how the two layers compose.
questions.caveat: On a single host the MPI layer adds no hardware; hybrid can only win by decomposing work better.

questions.question: Why was Hybrid 1×4 the strongest four-slot layout?
questions.short: It never partitions the tile list: every tile is split four ways inside, so the tile-level imbalance that caps static partitions does not arise.
evidence: Hybrid 1×4 vs OpenMP 4: -20.66% (CI -25.95% to -18.80%), faster in 7/7 blocks
Speedup 2.45× exceeds the 2.34× cap of the equal-count 4-way partition
questions.caveat: A decomposition effect, not evidence that hybrid is intrinsically faster. OpenMP with dynamic tile scheduling was not in the formal matrix.

questions.question: Why did dynamic scheduling help?
questions.short: The expensive tiles sit in one band. A static contiguous split gives that band to one worker; one-tile dynamic assignment lets both workers draw from the whole image, so neither is left with much more than one tile of extra work.
evidence: Fixed dynamic vs static: 27.5% to 31.8% faster on all 9 natural-scene cases; every interval excludes zero
With rank 1 slowed 2× (synthetic): -12.06%
questions.caveat: The scenes were designed to be uneven, which favours dynamic scheduling.

questions.question: Why did adaptive batching not consistently outperform fixed dynamic scheduling?
questions.short: Fixed dynamic already removed the imbalance, and on one host messages are cheap. Adaptive cut the number of assignments but the waiting it saved was a few milliseconds, smaller than run-to-run variation.
evidence: 8 of 10 adaptive-vs-fixed intervals include zero
The two that exclude zero point in opposite directions: medium uniform -2.73%; large reflective +1.83%
Assignments 28 to 100 instead of 144
Medium runs: worker assignment wait 9 to 10 ms (fixed) vs 3 to 7 ms (adaptive) per render
questions.caveat: This does not show adaptive batching would fail over a real network or with very small tiles; that was not tested.

questions.question: Why are static speedups only about 2× at four slots?
questions.short: The measured tile costs cap any equal-count contiguous split: the heaviest range sets the time even with perfect workers.
evidence: Cap 1.23× (2-way) and 2.34× (4-way) from the per-tile costs
Observed OpenMP 4 1.93×, MPI 4 1.95×
questions.caveat: A cost-aware split could do better; none of these backends uses one.

questions.question: What caused the hybrid performance anomaly?
questions.short: Two real defects: per-thread counters that false-shared cache lines (only the intra-tile hybrid path exposed it) and a heap-allocated BVH traversal stack on every ray query (a serial cost in every backend).
evidence: Historical hybrid 2×2 4.707 s vs OpenMP 4 3.208 s (+43.46%)
Counter fix alone: hybrid 2×2 -13.99%, sequential +0.05% (no change resolved)
Both fixes: sequential -44.62%, hybrid 2×2 -53.36%
Final hybrid 2×2 vs OpenMP 4: -0.30% (CI -2.02% to +3.29%), no clear difference established
questions.caveat: The historical 4.707 s was not reproduced by later rebuilds of the pre-fix source (3.72 to 4.02 s), so its full size was never attributed.

questions.question: Is hybrid 2×2 now as fast as OpenMP 4 and MPI 4?
questions.short: No clear difference was established. The intervals include zero; that is not proof of equality.
questions.caveat: Seven blocks give coarse intervals; the MPI interval only just contains zero, so a small penalty cannot be ruled out.

questions.question: Why is weak scaling described as single-host?
questions.short: SPP was raised in proportion to rendering slots on one laptop. That measures how extra cores on the same machine absorb extra work, not cluster scalability.
evidence: Weak efficiency at 4 slots: OpenMP 0.49, MPI 0.49, hybrid 2×2 0.48
questions.caveat: The same equal-count partitions are used, so these values mostly re-measure the spatial imbalance.

questions.question: How is deterministic correctness verified?
questions.short: Every timed run's image hash is compared with the sequential reference, formal images are rehashed independently, and the validators and core tests check backends, the BVH and edge cases.
evidence: 458 of 458 formal images rehashed, 0 failed
11 backend configurations · 6 BVH scenes · 12 CLI cases · 4 analysis tests
Intra-tile thread test fails on a deliberately racy counter mutant
questions.caveat: Equality is exact for this build and toolchain.

questions.question: What does the controlled DNF demonstrate?
questions.short: A deliberately oversized workload was run once under a supervisor with a planned 600 s limit. It ran until it was stopped, with no crash or error output, and the manifest records exactly what ran. Helios writes its image and statistics only when a render completes and prints no progress, so no partial image exists.
evidence: 1280×720 at 2048 SPP = 1,887,436,800 camera samples
Terminated at 600.34 s; stderr 0 bytes
questions.caveat: How far it got is unknown. Memory use was not recorded; the 8-bit RGB image buffer is about 2.8 MB.

questions.question: What are the main limits of the evaluation?
questions.short: One laptop (4 cores, 8 logical processors), single-host MPI, an uncontrolled Windows system, no temperature telemetry, synthetic heterogeneity and a small procedural scene catalogue.
evidence: Mitigations: warm-up, 7 randomised blocks, medians, paired bootstrap intervals, frozen source, independent hash checks, no removal of slow runs
questions.caveat: These limit generalisation, not the within-experiment comparisons.

source_note: Answers are grounded in the Helios technical report; every number is filled in from extracted evidence at build time.
